title: Reversing lists, cycle detection & the STL list
overview: This module applies linked-list skills to classic tasks: reversing a singly list with recursion, reversing a doubly list with two pointers, spotting a cycle with slow and fast pointers, and checking a palindrome. It then introduces C++'s ready-made doubly linked list, `std::list`, with its constructors, modifiers, operations and iterators. Once you can write these by hand, you know what the STL is doing for you.

concepts.term: Recursive reversal of a singly list
concepts.explain: Recurse to the last node and make it the new head. While returning, each node makes its next node point back at it (`temp->next->next = temp`) and clears its own `next`.

concepts.term: Two-pointer reversal of a doubly list
concepts.explain: Put `i` at the head and `j` at the tail, swap their values, and move them towards each other. Stop when they meet (odd length) or cross (`i->prev == j`, even length).
concepts.snippet: for(i=head, j=tail; i!=j && i->prev!=j; i=i->next, j=j->prev) swap(i->val, j->val);

concepts.explain: Same two pointers as the reversal, but compare instead of swap. One mismatch means the list is not a palindrome.
`slow` moves one step and `fast` moves two. If there is a loop, `fast` eventually lands on `slow`; if not, `fast` reaches `NULL`. Move first, then compare, because both start at the head.
concepts.snippet: while(fast && fast->next){ slow=slow->next; fast=fast->next->next; if(slow==fast) return true; }

concepts.explain: `list<int>` is a doubly linked list. It has O(1) `push_front`, `push_back`, `pop_front`, `pop_back`, `front()`, `back()`, `size()` and `empty()`. There is no `[]`; use iterators.
`l.begin()` points to the first element; `l.end()` points one past the last, so the last element is `*prev(l.end())` or `*(--l.end())`. `next(l.begin(), i)` walks i steps and takes O(i).
`l.insert(it, value)` or `l.insert(it, first, last)` puts values before `it`. `l.erase(it)` removes one element; `l.erase(a, b)` removes the half-open range [a, b).

`remove(v)` deletes every `v`; `sort()` sorts (pass `greater<int>()` for descending); `unique()` removes adjacent duplicates, so sort first; `reverse()` flips the order. `find` and `replace` come from `<algorithm>`.

files.title: Reverse a singly linked list (recursion)
files.what: Reads a list, prints it, reverses the actual links with a recursive function, and prints it again.
steps: `reverse_linked_list(head, tail, head)` recurses down with `temp->next`.
Base case: at the last node (`temp->next == NULL`), set `head = temp` — the old last node is the new head.
While returning, `temp->next->next = temp` turns the link around.
`temp->next = NULL` cuts the old forward link, and `tail = temp`; the final return leaves the old head as `tail`.
For 10 20 30 40: 40 becomes head, then 40→30, 30→20, 20→10, and 10→NULL.
files.complexity: Time O(n) · Space O(n) for the recursion stack
files.output_note: Under "Before reversing" you see 10 20 30 40; under "After reversing" you see 40 30 20 10 — the links really changed, not just the printing order.
files.watch_out: An empty list crashes, because `temp->next` is read when `temp` is `NULL`. Check `head == NULL` before calling.

check.q: Why is `temp->next = NULL` needed after flipping the link?
check.a: Otherwise the old head still points forward, making a two-node cycle at the end of the list.

files.title: Reverse a singly list (practice copy)
files.what: Same function, but `main` calls it with only two arguments, so it does not compile.
steps: Same recursive link reversal.
files.output_note: No output: compile error "too few arguments to function reverse_linked_list".
files.watch_out: The function takes `(head, tail, temp)`. Call `reverse_linked_list(head, tail, head);` instead of `reverse_linked_list(head, temp);`.

check.q: In the recursion, which node becomes the new head?
check.a: The old last node, set in the base case.

files.title: Reverse a doubly linked list (buggy main)
files.what: Reverses a doubly list by swapping values from both ends with `reverse_doubly`, but `main` never reads the list.
steps: `i` starts at `head`, `j` at `tail`.
While `i != j` (odd length) and `i->prev != j` (even length), swap `i->val` and `j->val`.
Move `i` forward and `j` backward.
`main` loops `while(tail)`, but `tail` is `NULL`, so nothing is read; both prints show an empty line.
files.output_note: Only blank lines — the list stays empty. After the fix you would see `10 20 30 40` then `40 30 20 10`.
files.watch_out: Write the input loop as `while(true)` with `break;` on -1 (not `return;`). Also, `reverse_doubly` would crash on an empty list because it reads `i->prev` when `i` is `NULL`.

check.q: For 4 nodes, why is `i != j` alone not enough to stop?
check.a: With an even length the pointers never meet; they cross, so we also stop when `i->prev == j`.

files.title: Reverse a doubly list (practice copy)
files.what: Adds a second approach, `reverse_doubly_1`, that swaps each node's `next` and `prev`, and uses the value-swap version (`reverse_doubly_2`) in `main`. The same `while(tail)` bug remains.
steps: `reverse_doubly_1`: for every node, `swap(tmp->next, tmp->prev)`, then move with `tmp = tmp->prev` (the old next).
At the end it swaps `head` and `tail`.
`reverse_doubly_2` is the two-pointer value swap.
files.output_note: Blank lines only, as in the original, because the input loop never runs.
files.watch_out: `reverse_doubly_1` takes `head` and `tail` by value, so its final `swap(head, tail)` is lost; use `Node* &head, Node* &tail`. The input loop needs `while(true)` and `break;`.

check.q: After swapping `next` and `prev` in a node, which pointer leads to the rest of the unprocessed list?
check.a: `prev`, because it now holds the old `next`.

files.title: Detect a cycle (slow and fast pointers)
files.what: Builds 10→20→30→40→50 and links 50 back to 20, then uses Floyd's slow/fast pointers to report whether a cycle exists.
steps: `slow` and `fast` both start at `head`.
While `fast` and `fast->next` exist, the loop checks `slow == fast`, then moves `slow` one step and `fast` two steps.
If they are equal, set `flag = true` and stop.
If `fast` runs off the end, there is no cycle.
Print "Cycle Detected" or "No Cycle".
files.output_note: `Cycle Detected`. The answer is right here, but only by luck — see the pitfall.
files.watch_out: The comparison happens before the first move, when `slow` and `fast` are both at `head`, so the program reports a cycle for every list with at least two nodes. Move both pointers first, then compare. Test it with `d->next = NULL`: it should say "No Cycle".

check.q: Why does `fast` always catch `slow` inside a loop?
check.a: Each step the gap between them shrinks by one, so it must reach zero.

files.what: Identical re-typing, including the compare-before-move bug.
steps: Same slow/fast loop.
files.watch_out: Same bug as the original: compare after moving the pointers.

check.q: What stops the loop when there is no cycle?

files.title: Compare two doubly lists (buggy)
files.what: Reads two doubly lists and compares their sizes (YES/NO). The input loops are broken, so it prints nothing.
steps: The first loop appends values to list 1 but runs `return;` on -1, ending the program.
The second loop uses `while(tail2)`, which would never run because `tail2` is `NULL`.
`get_size` counts nodes; equal sizes → YES.
files.complexity: Time O(n + m) · Space O(n + m)
files.output_note: Empty output: `main` returns as soon as the first -1 is read.
files.watch_out: Use `while(true)` with `break;` in both loops. Also, the practice task asks whether the lists are the *same*, which needs a value-by-value comparison after the size check, not only the sizes.

check.q: Lists `10 20 30` and `30 20 10`: what should a same-list check print?
check.a: NO — the sizes match but the values differ by position.

files.title: Is the doubly list a palindrome? (buggy main)
files.what: Compares values from both ends with two pointers and prints YES if the list reads the same both ways. `main` exits on -1 before checking.
steps: `i` from `head`, `j` from `tail`.
Loop while `i != j` and `i->prev != j`.
If `i->val != j->val`, set `flag = false` and stop.
Return `flag` and print YES/NO.
files.output_note: Empty output: `return;` on -1 ends `main` early. After the fix this input prints `YES`.
files.watch_out: Replace `return;` with `break;` in the input loop.

check.q: Is `10 20 30 30 20 10` a palindrome, and where do the pointers stop?
check.a: Yes; they stop when they cross between the two 30s (`i->prev == j`).

files.title: Palindrome check (practice copy)
files.what: Same idea, but `is_palindrome` was changed to return `void` and always `return true`, so it does not compile.
steps: Same two-pointer comparison.
files.output_note: No output: compile error "void value not ignored as it ought to be".
files.watch_out: Declare it `bool is_palindrome(...)` and `return flag;` (returning `true` would ignore the comparisons). Also change `return;` to `break;` in `main`.

check.q: What would `return true;` at the end make the function report?
check.a: Always YES, even for lists that are not palindromes.

files.title: `std::list` constructors and capacity
files.what: Tours the ways to create a `list<int>` (empty, N elements, N copies of V, initializer list, copy, from an array, from a vector) and the capacity functions `size`, `clear`, `empty` and `resize`.
steps: `list<int> l;` → size 0. `list<int> l2(10);` → 10 zeros. `list<int> l3(10, 5);` → ten 5s.
`front()`, `back()` and `*l3.begin()` all give 5.
`*(--l3.end())` is the last element; `l.end()` itself is one past the end.
`l5(l4.begin(), l4.end())`, `l6(l5)`, `l7(arr, arr+5)` and `l8(v.begin(), v.end())` copy from other containers.
`clear()` empties `l8`; `empty()` then returns true.
`l7.resize(10)` grows it to 10, filling the new places with 0.
files.complexity: Most calls O(1); constructing, copying, clear and resize are O(n)
files.output_note: Read top to bottom: 0, 10, 10, 5, 5, 5, then `10` from `*l3.end()` (a meaningless value), 5, 5, 1, 5, 5, the two loops over l5, `The list l7 is:` 1 2 3 4 5, 10 20 30 40 50, 0, `List is empty`, 10, and the resized `1 2 3 4 5 0 0 0 0 0`. The line `1 2 3 4 5 5` is the range-for over l5 glued to `l6.size()`, because no `endl` was printed between them.
files.watch_out: `*l3.end()` is undefined behaviour — `end()` is not an element. Never dereference it; use `*prev(l3.end())`.

files.title: `std::list` element access
steps: `l.front()` → first value; `l.back()` → last value.
`*next(l.begin(), 2)` walks two steps → the value at index 2.
`*l.begin()` is the same as `front()`.
`*(--l.end())` steps back from one-past-the-end → the last value.

check.q: Why can't you write `l[2]` for a `std::list`?
check.a: A linked list has no random access; reaching index 2 means walking, so the class does not offer `[]`.

files.title: `std::list` modifiers
files.what: Demonstrates copying, `assign`, push/pop at both ends, `insert` (one value or a range), `erase` (one element or a range), `replace`, `find` with `distance`, and `remove`, printing the list after each step.
steps: `list<int> l2 = l;` makes an independent copy: pushing onto `l` does not change `l2`.
`push_back`, `push_front`, `pop_back`, `pop_front` work at the ends in O(1).
`l.insert(next(l.begin(), 2), 100)` puts 100 before index 2; the range versions insert a whole list or vector there.
`l.erase(it)` removes one element; `l.erase(first, last)` removes [first, last).
`replace(l.begin(), l.end(), 1000, 999)` changes every 1000 to 999.
`find` returns an iterator (or `l.end()` if missing); `distance(l.begin(), it)` turns it into an index.
`l.remove(999)` deletes every 999.
files.output_note: Each message is followed by the list after that step. Useful checkpoints: after the inserts the list is `1 2 33 44 55 111 222 333 444 555 100 3 4 5`; 999 is found at index 8, 333 at index 2, and 45678 is not present; the final list is `2 44 333 444 555 100 3 4`.
files.watch_out: The message for `l.erase(next(l.begin(), 2), next(l.begin(), 5))` says it removes the 3rd and 4th elements, but the range [2, 5) removes three elements (indexes 2, 3, 4): 55, 111 and 222.

check.q: How many elements does `l.erase(next(l.begin(),1), next(l.begin(),4))` remove?

files.title: `std::list` operations: remove, sort, unique, reverse
files.what: Applies `remove`, `sort`, `sort(greater<int>())`, `unique`, `reverse` and `empty` to a list with repeated values.
steps: `l.remove(3)` deletes every 3.
`l.sort()` sorts ascending; `l.sort(greater<int>())` sorts descending.
`l.unique()` only removes *adjacent* duplicates, so the code sorts first.
`l.reverse()` flips the order.
`l.empty()` returns a bool, printed as 0 (false) or 1 (true).
files.complexity: remove/unique/reverse O(n) · sort O(n log n)
files.output_note: Lines: `1 2 40 30 40 30 4 5` (3s removed), `1 2 4 5 30 30 40 40` (ascending), `40 40 30 30 5 4 2 1` (descending), `1 2 4 5 30 40` (sorted then unique), `40 30 5 4 2 1` (reversed), and `Is the list l empty? 0`.
files.watch_out: The line `l.empty();` on its own does nothing — it only asks a question. To empty a list use `l.clear()`.

check.q: What does `unique()` leave for `{1, 2, 1, 1}` if you skip sorting?

recap: Recursive reversal: recurse first, then `temp->next->next = temp; temp->next = NULL;`.
Two pointers from both ends reverse or palindrome-check a doubly list; stop on meet or cross.
Floyd's cycle check: move slow by 1 and fast by 2, then compare.
`std::list` is a doubly linked list: O(1) at the ends, no `[]`, use `next(it, i)`.
`end()` is one past the last element — never dereference it.

check_yourself.q: What is the extra space cost of the recursive singly-list reversal, and how could you avoid it?
check_yourself.a: O(n) for the call stack; an iterative version with `prev`, `curr` and `next` pointers uses O(1).

check_yourself.q: Why can't `std::sort` be used on a `std::list`?
check_yourself.a: `std::sort` needs random-access iterators; a list only has bidirectional ones, so it provides its own `l.sort()`.

check_yourself.q: In cycle detection, why must the pointers move before they are compared?
check_yourself.a: They both start at the head, so comparing first would always find them equal and wrongly report a cycle.
It inserts 5 before the first element — the same as `push_front(5)`.
